izig4x:331: The logic of Prompt is "telling AI what to do"—giving rules, giving examples, giving constraints, and AI executes according to instructions. The logic of Skill is "solidifying human experience"—how does this person judge? What are their judgment criteria? How do they weigh trade-offs when encountering contradictions? The AI behaviors produced by these two logics differ fundamentally: Prompt-driven AI output depends on the model's own reasoning ability, while Skill-driven AI output replicates this person's judgment framework. The core change in the third round of debugging—from "giving constraints" to "giving judgment logic"—precisely illustrates this point. Ratio constraints are shallow rules; when AI executes them, it does not understand the business logic behind the ratio. Judgment logic (no hours if requirements are unclear; break down by scenario chain rather than guessing by role) is the true core of experience. Only when AI learns this logic can it make reasonable judgments in new scenarios, instead of mechanically applying ratios.
j0nwsm:227: is the second most common mistake. Rules tell AI "what" (testing is 1/3–1/2 of backend), while framework tells AI "why" (why the ratio is reasonable, and when it does not apply). Rules without framework are fragile—when AI encounters edge cases, it neither knows why the rule exists nor can it adjust flexibly. The deeper problem: AI is far stronger at executing rules than understanding them. This is why an "obedient" AI produced more dogmatic results—AI faithfully executed every rule, but each rule was executed in isolation without considering the interacting context, so the final result ended up further from the empirical value.
